title: I've released 23 small mobile games in about six months as a solo dev. Here's how it actually works
author: office-canard
selftext:
I run a one-person studio making small mobile games, and I've released 23 of them in roughly the last six months. People sometimes ask how that's possible, so here's an honest breakdown, sorted by stage.

1. Ideas

Most of my ideas come from everyday life.

\- I was in the hospital and had to ride a wheelchair, and I wanted to tear around in it. That became WHEELCHAIR D, a wheelchair racing game.

\- An Uber Eats driver told me waiting for elevators was a pain, and I wanted to control elevators efficiently. That became LOOK EV.

\- I saw a windfoil on TV and wanted to ride one. That became FOIL OF THE DEAD.

\- I was searching for something in my room and wanted to tilt the whole room and slide everything out of the way at once. That became TILT ROOM.

I don't decide the core of a game before I start. I build a rough prototype that just about works. If it looks like it could become something, I keep going. If not, I drop it. I've thrown away several times more ideas than I've actually finished.

2. Production

It varies a lot. Some games have the whole system working in a day, and after that it's just making stage variations. Others take two months of wandering around. SYZYGY RUNNER started out as a pulley-based cargo-lifting puzzle and ended up as a side-scrolling action game.

My role is basically project lead and director. In the past I would have hired a musician for music, an illustrator for art and a coder for code, and managed all of them. Now I give those same jobs to AI.

I usually work on two or more games at once. Since I set my own deadlines, I just pick whichever one I feel like working on. Running an action game and a puzzle game side by side is great for switching gears. Right now, though, I'm making two puzzle games and both are in the debugging phase, so all I do all day is solve puzzles. It's a pain.

3. Finishing and testing

I don't think there's such a thing as a perfect or complete game. So I ask myself: if I'd had a smartphone in middle school, would I have played this? If the answer is yes, I ship it.

For puzzles, whether a stage can be solved, and for action games, whether a jump can be made and how many tenths of a second of leeway there are: I have AI calculate those. But in the end, a game is all about how it feels in your hands, so the numbers are just there to back that up.

4. Review and release

I've never failed review on Android. iOS is different. When I submitted several apps close together, they got flagged as spam, and it really looked like nobody had played them. I didn't find any magic trick. I just kept politely asking them to actually look at what was in the games.

Honestly, the place where AI helped me most was preparing release builds and figuring out the submission process. When there's a correct answer, AI is incredibly efficient at finding it and building it. Game design has no correct answer, so in the end, that part is still up to me.

Why small games? I just like small things that run on systems. Also, big games need a massive amount of debugging, and that scares me.

5. Marketing

Right now Instagram gets by far the most response. What surprised me is that a single raw run, failures and all, gets a much bigger reaction than a highlight video I edited myself. I'm still learning how X works.

The thing I struggle with most is getting reviews.

6. Keeping it going

My actual working hours haven't changed from when I made things with people. My collaborators are just faster now, so things come out sooner.

Game making is a hobby for me, and I do it within that. I probably have more free time than someone with a regular job. Also, I don't have many friends, so my calendar never fills up with dinners or barbecues.

It's not that I'm trying to pump out a lot of games. It's more that each time one gets done, I want people to play it, and that has just added up.

A question for you

Who are you making your games for?

For me, the one who decides whether a game is finished is middle-school me. But the player I'm actually imagining is old-man me. That's probably why I keep making games with simple rules that anyone can play. Big RPGs take a lot of stamina, you know?

Happy to answer any questions.

comments.author: wisedingus
comments.body:
Nice, this is pretty cool. Few questions:  
\- How many installs has your highest installed game accumulated? Average installs?  
\- How are you monetizing - IAP/ads/etc.? How much revenue has your studio generated from all of these games?

Even just ballpark is fine, curious if AI game dev is sustainable as a business yet.

replies.author: Three_Tails_Studio
replies.body:
Of course AI game dev is sustainable as a business but you need to be developing good ideas with human soul and heart. 

You aren’t going to one shot your way to success.

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body:
Not even close yet. None of my games has reached 100 downloads. Ads are my only source of revenue.



I'm a one-person studio, so whether it turns into a business really comes down to whether I can get the word out. I'm confident in the games themselves, though.

replies.author: Chocoweb88
replies.body: how do you get ads revenue without downloads?

replies.author: ImCallingYouOutOnBS
replies.body: He probably does, but a very small amount. Like, $2 per game

replies.author: VihmaVillu
replies.body:
After making few of them with less than 100 downloads why you kept going and didnt refine/tune the ones you already made?  
Why not put this effort to getting players?  
Its very possible that the approach sucks and you just keep making failed games nobody likes

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body:
I've thought about what happens when you keep polishing something alone, and I don't think it ever leads anywhere good.



Of course every game is properly playable and fun. But once it reaches the point where I want other people to judge it, I release it.



I don't have friends, and I'm not part of any community yet. That's what I'm starting to work on now. Remember, I've only been making games for six months. A store release is simply the way for my games to be seen by the most people.



Let me say it again.



I don't have any friends.

replies.author: VihmaVillu
replies.body:
why you keep mentioning friends here? how that matters in any way here?

*"I've thought about what happens when you keep polishing something alone, and I don't think it ever leads anywhere good."*  
I'm sorry dude but this is so wrong that I'm almost out of words.  
Most probably you just don't know what needs polishing and thats why you need players who will tell you that. Make discord channel and direct player there. It only takes 1 player who takes their time and writes you ideas/feedback/bug reports

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body:
I think we actually agree. That's exactly what I meant: polishing alone, without anyone telling me what's wrong, doesn't work. I don't have friends or a community who can play my games before release, so putting them out on the store is how I find those players.



The Discord idea is a good one. Thanks.

replies.author: hydroxyHU
replies.body:
Perhaps investing six months into a single game, focusing on polishing it, validating the concept, and building an audience around it, would have produced a much more valuable result than releasing 23 games that barely anyone has downloaded.

Development speed isn't necessarily the bottleneck. Sometimes it's product validation, marketing, and distribution.

replies.author: chesserios
replies.body: Time to invest in some marketing mate.

replies.author: brightfutureman
replies.body:
Yes, I’m curious about some numbers too. 

Overall, sounds interesting, OP.

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body: About one chicken's worth so far. Can't afford the mustard sauce yet.

comments.author: Massivemployer25
comments.body:
A few questions:

1. Are you monetizing?

2. Do you ever recycle stuff? Code, UIs, game mechanics etc.

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body:
1. Yes, but ads only. No in-app purchases.

2. Yes. The ad setup is pretty much shared across all of them. Some games reuse a format and some are built from scratch. For example, TILT ROOM, SNOWBALL FIELDS and SHADE PLOP are puzzles that play in completely different ways, but they use almost the same format.

comments.author: GurCalm
comments.body: What harness are you using, and any external tools/skills? Or is the whole pipeline besides the model in-house?

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body:
Nothing fancy. I just use the regular Claude chat in the browser (claude.ai), with Projects, on Opus 5.5. No special harness, no external tools or skills.



Claude pushes the code to GitHub, and the game goes live from there. It also tests the physics and game logic in Node.js before I play anything. That part wasn't my idea, though. Claude just started doing it on its own.



For art, sometimes I have AI generate it, sometimes I use Mixamo, and sometimes other assets. Same for sound.

comments.author: office-canard
comments.body:
A few people asked what these games actually are, so here's the full list. If any of them sounds interesting, I'd really appreciate it if you gave it a try.



1. WHEELCHAIR D (racing)

Two hands, two wheels. A wheelchair racing game where each wheel has its own lever. Chase world records across 31 courses, or take on three rivals in Battle.



2. HAMMER FROG (3D puzzle)

A frog with a hammer, stranded atop a tower in the sky. Knock the blocks out level by level and make your way back down to the river. Pull them in the wrong order and you strand yourself.



3. must be one (number puzzle)

Tap, solve, and turn every tile into one. Easy to pick up, endlessly deep.



4. PROBE GRAVITY (gravity puzzle)

Red planets pull, blue ones push. Bend gravity and guide your probe home along a single line. 100 stages.



5. RIDING SHOTGUN (shooter)

A getaway with the bride you stole. From the shotgun seat of a speeding car, gun down the bikes and enemies closing in.



6. EPURER (3D puzzle)

Rotate the solid, read its shape, and strip away what isn't needed. A minimal puzzle built for quiet thinking.



7. LOOK EV (elevator sim)

You're the dispatcher. Run the elevator and clear the daily rush.



8. FREIGHT FRIGHT (timing puzzle)

Grab cargo, load the cart, and send it off at the perfect moment. A race against the clock.



9. GYRO CHOPPER (dogfight)

Master the weight, loop behind, and cash in. A momentum-driven aerial dogfight.



10. HOOK UP! (climbing action)

Throw the hook, swing, dodge, and haul yourself up the tower. Vertical arcade action.



11. SCOPE & LANDMINE (turn-based defense)

Aim. Fire. Defend your PC. Snipe the AI invaders before they get through.



12. TURTLE, HOMEBOUND (journey)

One endless sea, the long way home, and someone slower swimming beside you. Read the currents and cross dawn after dawn back to the shore you came from. No death, no fail, no ads.



13. SMART VOID (aim & merge)

Launch balls, merge them into bigger ones, and knock down the invaders closing in. Endless waves.



14. UNMIRROR (room escape)

Find your way out of quiet, mirrored rooms. Behind each door, something is slightly off.



15. 16bars (music)

Tap along with the chords and your notes turn into an improvised line. A jam session that needs no training.



16. SEIZE (board game)

No trapping needed: place a piece next to your opponent's and the neighbors flip to your color. Gimmick cells, ever-harder stages, and a stage editor.



17. REBEL LEVEL (valve puzzle)

Tanks joined by pipes, and every lever works exactly once. Read the order before you touch anything, and bring every tank to the red line. 256 basins, no timer.



18. FOIL OF THE DEAD (windfoil shooter)

A resort sea full of zombies. No engine: read the wind, rise onto the foil and fly, then shoot as you sail. Seven seas, one stick and one FIRE button.



19. SHADE PLOP (shadow puzzle)

Hop from shadow to shadow and get the little frogs home. The sun never waits, and every beat the shadows swing a little further.



20. TILT ROOM (tilt puzzle)

Night in a child's bedroom. Tilt the floor and everything slides at once, the bear, the blocks, the toy cars. Find the right order and roll the bear out the door. 500 rooms.



21. SNOWBALL FIELDS (snowball puzzle)

Snow makes it grow, dirt makes it melt. Roll the snowball to exactly the size your little sister holds up, and build a snowman together. 300 fields.



22. SYZYGY RUNNER (cyber action runner)

Stop, and you're deleted. Run through a glowing cyberspace while your twin pistols fire on their own. Ride ropes, zip lines, trebuchets and cannons. 100 clusters.



23. APE SCALES (balance puzzle)

Hang coconuts on a mobile of bars and ropes until every bar is level. Then the ape jumps on, and that's your final answer. 100 stages, each with exactly one solution.



Coming soon



24. FIRE MOAT (firefighting puzzle)

The missiles have hit and the fire is spreading. Grab a shovel and dig: water fills every hole, and fire can never cross water. But each shovel works only once, the missiles keep falling, and an armory can blow the fire across the river. Count the turns, find the one route, and save everyone.



25. LITTLE PIVOT (moving puzzle)

Two little bears run a tiny moving team. Furniture only goes forward or back, never sideways. Turn it around one end, swap ends, turn again, and the impossible sofa slides right through the door. 256 days, from January to Christmas.



All free on Google Play, and most are on the App Store too: [https://www.office-canard.com/](https://www.office-canard.com/)
